title: Wren and the Gravity
premise: Kestrel Villalobos is a clone who inherited her original's unsolved murder case and a cargo hauler, scraping a living on the margins of contested space. When she intercepts a distress signal in a language extinct for two centuries, she realizes it's addressed to her original—and that answering it will expose the clone registry fraud keeping her alive. Racing to a derelict relay at the edge of dead space, she discovers the signal comes from another clone of herself, one who never fled, and who has spent three years being interrogated by the people who murdered the original. Kestrel must choose between destroying the evidence that could clear her name and saving the only person who shares her memories, and in the end she sacrifices her anonymity—broadcasting her own existence to save her sister-copy, accepting that survival means finally being seen.
about_author: Zephyrine Whitlock is the pen name of a former orbital logistics analyst who spent six years writing technical manuals before turning to fiction. She lives in a coastal town where she restores antique radios and insists the future will smell like ozone and salt.

chapters.title: Dead Weight
chapters.summary: Kestrel's POV. A routine cargo run through contested orbits establishes her careful invisibility: forged transponder, borrowed name, three years since the original's murder. She pays off a dock inspector with contraband coffee and reflects on how clones inherit debts, not lives. Emotional beat: weary vigilance, the loneliness of a person legally forbidden to exist.

chapters.title: A Language With No Speakers
chapters.summary: Kestrel's POV. Drifting near a dead relay, her rig catches a repeating signal in Old Meridian—a language extinct since the Diaspora Wars. Decryption reveals coordinates and one phrase: 'Kestrel, come home.' Only her original spoke it. She should delete it; instead she plots the course. Emotional beat: dread curdling into irresistible hope.

chapters.title: The Registry Problem
chapters.summary: Alternating POV: Inspector Dae-Sun Okonkwo, a registry auditor, flags an anomaly—two identical biometric signatures pinging eleven light-minutes apart. He requests a pursuit warrant. Meanwhile Kestrel bribes a fuel-depot clerk and learns someone else asked about her ship last week. Emotional beat: the net tightening while she pretends it isn't.

chapters.title: Cargo of Ghosts
chapters.summary: Kestrel's POV. Alone in deep transit, she replays inherited memories—the original's last recorded day—to find why anyone would kill a cartographer. She discovers her original had mapped something in dead space and hidden the charts inside a children's lullaby. Emotional beat: grief for a woman whose memories feel like wearing someone else's coat.

chapters.title: Interrogation Room, Year Three
chapters.summary: Second clone's POV (unnamed). Held aboard the survey vessel Cassiopeia's Mercy, she has endured three years of questioning about the murder and the hidden charts. Her captors believe she knows where they are. She doesn't—but she knows the signal went out, and she knows what Kestrel will do. Emotional beat: defiant endurance sharpening into cold calculation.

chapters.title: The Toll at Thessaly Gate
chapters.summary: Kestrel's POV. At a checkpoint station, Okonkwo corners her—not with arrest, but with an offer: help him find the murderer and he'll lose her file. She refuses, lies badly, and barely clears the gate as his warrant processes. Emotional beat: terror mixed with the first flicker of trust in an enemy.

chapters.title: Dead Space, Live Signal
chapters.summary: Kestrel's POV. The relay at the edge of dead space is a cathedral of frozen bodies and failing lights—the site of the original's murder, preserved by vacuum. Following the lullaby-charts, she finds the hidden cache and, inside it, proof the original was killed for discovering a sanctioned massacre. Emotional beat: horror transmuting into purpose.

chapters.title: Two of One
chapters.summary: Both clones' POVs converge. The Cassiopeia's Mercy arrives; the second clone engineers her own escape during the chaos, reaching the relay wounded. Face to face, they share memories like passing a flame—each completing gaps in the other. Emotional beat: overwhelming recognition, love without romance, kinship beyond law.

chapters.title: Gravity Well
chapters.summary: Climax. Okonkwo's strike team boards; the second clone is recaptured. Kestrel faces the choice: flee with the evidence or broadcast everything—the massacre, the murder, her own illegal existence—on every open channel. She broadcasts, using her own exposure as the price of truth, and Okonkwo, seeing the full record, turns his weapons on his own command. Emotional beat: sacrifice as liberation.

chapters.title: What Survives
chapters.summary: Resolution, both clones' POVs. The broadcast ignites scandal across the contested orbits; the sisters are fugitives now, but no longer invisible—thousands of clones begin sending signals in Old Meridian. They load the rescued second clone's belongings aboard and plot a course together, two women sharing one name and choosing new ones. Emotional beat: hard-won peace, identity claimed rather than inherited.
